title: Love poured out (Romans 5:5–8)
hookLine: the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts, while we were yet sinners
last: ALL HAVE SINNED, ALL ARE LOVED.

lines: WOULD YOU DIE FOR A STRANGER?
THE MATH THAT DOESN'T ADD UP.
cards: Would you die for a stranger? Most people hope they'd be brave, but don't really know. For a good person, someone kind, someone you admire?

Maybe. Paul thinks about this out loud in Romans 5, like a man doing math on a napkin. Then he lands on something that doesn't add up at all: someone who died for people who weren't good, and weren't his friends yet.

teach.b: Start with verse five, in the Douay-Rheims: "the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts, by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us." Charity is the old English word for love, the Latin caritas, the Greek agape.
And it's poured. Not measured out in spoonfuls, not earned drop by drop. Poured, like water from a jug, until it runs over.
Paul says this is why hope doesn't disappoint: the love is already inside, given. Then the napkin math.

Scarcely would anyone die for a righteous man; for a good man someone might dare to die. But: "God commendeth his charity towards us; because when as yet we were sinners, according to the time, Christ died for us."
In the older English many people know: while we were yet sinners. Not after we cleaned up. Not once we deserved it.
While we were still a mess, still far off, still not his friends.
That's the order Paul insists on: love first, then change. Not change first, then love.
Catholics speak of this as grace, a gift given before any merit, and the Catechism quotes verse five when it calls love the Holy Spirit's first gift.
Notice what it does to the face in the mirror: your worst day was not a day you were unloved. And to everyone else: no one you meet is outside the reach of while we were yet sinners.

how: Catholics speak of grace as God's free gift, poured into the soul at baptism, and Romans 5 is among the readings the Church offers for confirmation, when it prays for the Holy Spirit.

who pours the love into our hearts

s: Paul says God loves people once they've cleaned up their lives
while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. love first, then change.
charity in the Douay-Rheims means love, not just giving money
it's the Latin caritas and the Greek agape.
Paul says someone might dare to die for a good person
then he says God's love went further: for sinners.

games.q: someone who has wronged you comes to you in need, before any apology. what do you do?
o: help, but remind them what they did.
games.why: not graded. but the pattern Paul describes is love first, while we were yet sinners, and change afterward.

practice: Remember a time someone was kind to you when you didn't deserve it: a parent after you'd slammed a door, a friend you'd let down, a stranger on a bad day.
Let it be true without explaining it away, then imagine love poured out like water on you exactly as you are, nothing fixed first. If you pray, simply say thank you.

wordCard.voice: Poured. Not measured in spoonfuls but poured out, like water from a jug, until it runs over: God's charity in our hearts. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love, the self-giving love Paul says is poured into our hearts. the Latin is caritas, charity.
